issue.body:
Keep `ChunkedXContent` objects for as long as we can, only iterate them when we actually need to.

Relates https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/118647

body: The previous API was very non-obvious and confusing to use, and it was unclear what each method in `ChunkedXContentHelper` was actually doing. I think there's a middle ground to find here, developing a good API whilst keeping the performance hit to a minimum. The changes in #118649 should ease the immediate performance hit in the meantime.

@thecoop those changes will help a little but not much I would expect, partly due to https://bugs.openjdk.org/browse/JDK-8267359. https://bugs.openjdk.org/browse/JDK-8267758 I'd say makes the stream approach bound to fail here.

Fundamentally there is no nice solution here, of that I'm quite convinced. The problem we have is the same you have in e.g. Netty serializers. If you want accurate chunk sizes, you need a low overhead `next` method. The nested custom iterators we have are (short of using code generation like tricks like manually building callsites) probably as good as it gets.
The last comment in the JDK issue I linked (https://bugs.openjdk.org/browse/JDK-8267359?focusedId=14426679&page=com.atlassian.jira.plugin.system.issuetabpanels%3Acomment-tabpanel#comment-14426679)  explains why there is no neat solution here I believe.

This API also doesn't have to be nicely usable. It is designed for the very narrow use case of very large REST responses. We should, going forward, not add new APIs that require this logic (I believe this was consensus when we added chunked encoding). This is to support existing debug style APIs like the cluster state where we have large responses by design and BwC makes it impossibly costly to change the design. Building the APIs from scratch I'd go as far as saying the search APIs are the only use case where chunked encoding just makes sense. So if we're not changing anything about this code and it's so extremely performance critical, why introduce the risk of stuff like this? We've seen how easy it is to accidentally regress massively once you introduce indirection to this logic haven't we? :)
